def: Secondary products produced in addition to the principal product. In meat, this includes organs, blood, and bone. Not inherently bad, but often indicates lower quality control than named organ meats.
Food that has had its moisture removed using low heat over a long period. Creates a chewy texture.
Food that has been frozen, then placed in a vacuum to remove moisture. Retains cellular structure better than dehydration and creates a crumbly texture.
A sweet, syrupy liquid often used as a binder and preservative in soft, chewy dog treats. While generally recognized as safe, it adds empty calories.
A marketing term legally meaning the product is made in a facility approved for human food production. It does not guarantee the food is biologically appropriate for dogs.
A diet or treat with a very short list of ingredients, usually one novel protein and one carbohydrate, used to diagnose or manage food allergies.
A protein source the dog has never eaten before (e.g., kangaroo, venison, rabbit), often used for dogs with common allergies to chicken or beef.
A product containing exactly one item, with no preservatives, binders, or fillers. E.g., '100% Beef Liver'.
The inner layer of cow or horse hide that is chemically treated, bleached, and glued into shapes. Highly dangerous due to blockage risks.
The stomach lining of ruminating animals (like cows or sheep). Extremely stinky but considered a superfood for dogs due to digestive enzymes.
A highly digestible, single-ingredient chew made from beef pizzle. A safe alternative to rawhide.
The windpipe of a cow, sheep, or pig. A crunchy, cartilaginous chew that is a natural source of glucosamine and chondroitin.
A treat that is incredibly motivating to a dog (usually smelly meat or cheese), used for teaching difficult behaviors or in highly distracting environments.
Dry dog food that is extruded and baked. Usually considered a 'low value' treat in training.
The mandatory labeling on pet food that lists the minimum percentages of crude protein and crude fat, and maximum percentages of crude fiber and moisture.
Meat that has been rendered (cooked down) to remove moisture and fat, resulting in a highly concentrated protein powder.
An extremely broad FDA term for flavor derived from natural sources. It provides no nutritional value.
Substances added to food to prevent spoilage. Natural preservatives include mixed tocopherols (Vitamin E); artificial ones include BHA and BHT.
A process of cooking animal by-products to separate fat, remove water, and kill bacteria.
A brand name often associated with using avocados, which requires careful processing as the pit and skin contain persin, which is toxic to dogs.
Compounds that prevent cellular damage. Often added to premium dog treats using blueberries or spinach.
Essential fats (often found in salmon or flaxseed) that reduce inflammation and improve coat health.
